utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's three 92 bis witnesses today, but before we come to those, can I respectfully remind the Chamber that the witness we seek to call tomorrow is subject to an application yet to be resolved, and I didn't know if the Chamber was in a position to assist us for planning purposes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Which witness is that?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Van Baal

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Van Baal. We will let you have a decision this morning. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should like for the record to say that I don't think it is in order -- actually, I don't think what Mr. Nice said on Thursday was in order, while I wasn't here, because he said that I have some sort of scheme according to which -- and pattern, which is why I was absent on Thursday. From that, it would emerge that I myself, according to this pattern, organised every day last week to have been kept here for several hours, which means that I myself curtailed my time for rest and preparation, and it would appear, according to that logic, that I organised the prolongation of the work here. And quite simply, I should like to state that that kind of statement on a moral and intellectual level at which this so-called entire -- so-called indictment is based. And for you I have a criticism personally, Mr. May, because you drew conclusions without having --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm not going to listen to this, Mr. Milosevic. In your absence, a comment was made by the Prosecutor as to a pattern of your illness. He went no further than that and made no further suggestions. If he had done, we would have ordered something to be done about it. As for any other orders we may have made, we will consider the position. We now have a medical report, and we'll consider the position further. Now, have you got any other submissions?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I was just going to say, Mr. May, that before you collected all the pertinent information, you drew conclusions, and you could have come by that information from your staff, either from the detention centre or the medical staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Yes. We will have the next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: The Prosecution would like to call Witness B-1058.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Your Honour, in the meantime, perhaps, since we're waiting for the witness to come, Your Honours have all been distributed with a package. Would Your Honours be so kind as perhaps to give that an exhibit number, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We'll get the next exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit number P531.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Perhaps the registrar would note we'll do without the P numbers in this case. I know other cases do, but we don't. Just give it -- Prosecution numbers get the straight number. 531.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: I'd just like to clarify, Your Honours; it should be tendered under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. If the witness would take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. If you'd take a seat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We can raise the blinds and go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd like to show the witness her pseudonym sheet, which can be found at tab number 1 of your package.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We can do that, but is there any reason why the blinds should not be raised? Can we raise them, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Witness, is that your name on the top of that sheet, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1058
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: And that sheet has been signed by you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1058
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Could I kindly also please show the witness the 92 bis package. This can be found at tab 2, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Witness, is this the statement you made before investigators of the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1058
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: And, Witness, is this also the statement which you certified and declared before the court officers of the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1058
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd also like to show the witness a document that is at tab 4 of your binder. Tab 3. I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Witness, is this a document which you have made and also signed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1058
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is a 92 bis witness, so if it pleases Your Honours, I'll just briefly read out the essence of the witness's testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: At the time of the incidents mentioned in this summary, the witness had been living in Zvornik with her husband and two sons for the last 20 years. Prior to the war in Zvornik, a majority of the population were Muslim. In 1991, the witness saw the fall of Vukovar in Croatia on Belgrade television. At the time, she could hardly believe this and thought that she was watching old World War II footage. In March 1992, she saw on television the events in Bijeljina, which again she could hardly believe. However, her sister, who was living in Bijeljina, told the witness that it was true and that their other sister's two sons had been murdered outside the garrison in Bijeljina. The first indications of the spreading of war to Zvornik occurred a few days before the attack on Zvornik when there was small-arms fire coming from Mali Zvornik and the arrival of tanks in the area. On April the 8th, negotiations were held in Mali Zvornik with Arkan, who represented the Serbs. Witness B-1237 was present who, after the meeting, came to the witness and told her that the situation was grave and advised her to leave.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please slow down, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: I beg your pardon, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You're being asked to slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. The witness, however, decided to stay as she had Serb friends and had not done anything wrong. The attack on Zvornik commenced later in the evening when Zvornik was shelled from Mali Zvornik. The witness and other people who were living in her apartment block in Filipa Kljajica Street took cover in the cellar of the building. The cellar became full. In the cellar there were about 12 men, 15 to 16 women, three children and two babies. In the morning at about 10.00, the witness heard a strong detonation and the door to the cellar was exploded open. Immediately after the door was opened, about ten soldiers wearing camouflage uniforms, black wooly hats rolled down as masks, and fingerless gloves burst into the cellar and threatened them with long rifles. The witness could tell that they were Serbs by their accents. The people in the cellar were told to hand over their weapons and the men were ordered outside to be searched. No one in the cellar had any weapons, not even a pocket knife. The women and children were rushed out of the cellar. However, the witness saw the men from the cellar with their hands on their heads and with their backs facing the apartment building. The witness was the last person out of the cellar and was ordered not to look round and to go to the SUP building. One soldier forced the witness to move by putting a rifle to her back and cursed her. After the witness had walked about 20 kilometres [sic] from the cellar, she heard a simultaneous burst of gunfire from behind. The witness tried to look around, but the soldiers poked her in the back with the rifles and prevented her from doing so. According to the witness, the gunshots could only have come from the area outside the apartment building where the men from the cellar were lined up. On the way to the SUP building, the witness saw two dead bodies lying outside houses. Loud Chetnik music was also being played out of cassette players as the witness walked down the street. The witness and the others were made to go inside the library which is opposite the SUP building where other soldiers were abusive to them and cursing Alija Izetbegovic. The soldiers in the library told the witness that they were Seselj's men and that they were the good guys and that all the killings had been done by Arkan's men. The witness knew that this was not true as Seselj's men had also fully participated in the killing of the men in the cellar. Whilst the witness was in the library, a Serb woman named Vera was allowed by the soldiers to go back to the apartment building to change her clothes. When Vera came back, she told another lady in the library that she had seen the awful sight of the dead bodies of the men who had been taken out of the cellar. Other women who later arrived in the library also said that they had seen the dead bodies of the witness's men outside their apartment building. Later in the day, Arkan came to the library and told them that he would send buses to pick them up. The buses arrived on the same day, and the witness and the others were herded onto them. Whilst travelling through Zvornik, the witness saw many other dead bodies lying in the garden of houses. Before the bus left Zvornik, four men were taken off the bus. The witness never saw these men again. The witness was dropped off in Banja Koviljaca in Serbia. About a week later, the witness and a friend returned to Zvornik to find out what had happened to the bodies of their men. The witness was directed to the Serb headquarters in Karakaj where their commander told her that the men she was looking for were not on any of their lists and she could go home. As the witness was leaving to walk the three kilometres back into Zvornik, she saw a truck which was about to leave, and the commander told the witness to get a lift back on the truck. The soldiers in the truck, however, were not prepared to take the "balijas," so they had to walk on foot. The witness then went to see Grujic who was president of the Serb municipality. Grujic, however, told the witness that he could not help her and that there was no longer a place for Muslims in Zvornik. The witness briefly went back to her own apartment block and at the spot where she had last seen the men from the cellar saw her husband's hat and one of her son's sports shoes on the ground covered in blood. There was also blood which was peppered bullet holes on the walls. On the ground, the witness also saw a number of spent bullets and three or four garotte wires. Of the men who were taken from the cellar and killed outside, one was the witness's husband and two others were her sons, aged 22 and 24 at that time. Now, if Your Honours may permit me, I would just like to show, under seal, one or two exhibits and ask the witness to comment on those.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Now, the first photograph is at tab number 4, and I would kindly ask the witness, please, to tell me if she can identify who that person is in the picture.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1058
utterances.text: My husband. My husband.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: And could I also please ask the witness to look at the picture which is in tab number 5 and ask the witness, please, to identify the people in that picture if she can.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1058
utterances.text: My two sons.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: And finally, I would like to show the witness another picture which has already previously been tendered.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1058
utterances.text: Arkan and that other associate of his. I don't know what his name is. But one is Arkan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Is there an exhibit number for that exhibit, Mr. Agha.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. 414, tab 1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. That finishes the evidence in chief for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, before I start examining this witness, I have a question. In point 7 of the statement, mention is made of a man by name and surname, somebody who attended negotiations in Zvornik, in actual fact. Now, is that a protected name or not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I don't recognise it for the minute, but I will ask Mr. Agha's assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Your Honour, that indeed is a protected witness who has already given evidence in these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Yes, it's protected then.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is it the protected witness who Mr. Agha Khan mentioned under pseudonym of 1237? Is that the one?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will get it checked.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, protective measures.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam 1058, I'm just going to ask you questions which I consider to be important in order to establish the truthfulness of this. I shall do my best not to hurt you with any of my questions in view of the fact that you lost your husband and your son, according to what it says here in your statement.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1058
utterances.text: Two sons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said that on Belgrade television in 1991, you saw the station reporting about the events in Vukovar, and in March 1992, a film, as you say, about the war in Bijeljina; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1058
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You yourself say that you believed that it was intimidation, instilling fear and that that was something -- some footage from World War II; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1058
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you learnt about both these events via Belgrade television, and you didn't actually believe what you were seeing; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1058
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You also say, in paragraph 5, that your sister, who lived in Bijeljina, in a telephone conversation told you that she was so frightened that she couldn't exactly tell you what was happening in Bijeljina; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1058
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, is it also true that the sons of your sister were also killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1058
utterances.text: Of my other sister, not the one I -- not this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You mean not the one you were talking to on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1058
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us the circumstances under which they were killed? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1058
utterances.text: Well, they were killed because Arkan's men took them away to the garrison, and the children later asked to go and see their grandmother to tell her where they were and that they would come back straight away. The children did come back, but in coming back, they shot at them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who shot at them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1058
utterances.text: I wasn't there, so I didn't see it myself, but they were killed by Arkan's men and by the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did anybody tell you who shot at them of the people who were there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1058
utterances.text: Well, nobody was there when they killed them. They just met them on the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How many people were killed in Bijeljina, lost their lives?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1058
utterances.text: I don't know. I can't say. But many people died. How many exactly, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say, paragraph 6, that you didn't know until the very outbreak of the conflict in Zvornik that the conflict would take place; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1058
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it also true that everyone else was saying that there would be no conflict?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1058
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then you say that there were negotiations and that a man who had the pseudonym 1237 here and who was an official in Zvornik attended; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1058
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you know that also because later on that same man who attended the negotiations came to your house and told you that it had been agreed that the Muslims should surrender their weapons; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1058
utterances.text: He said that things would not be good and that we should flee.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: He told you to flee or that it wouldn't be a good thing for you to flee?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1058
utterances.text: He told us to flee, that things would not be good.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you say in paragraph 7 that this man, after that meeting, "came to our house and told us that it had been agreed that the Muslims surrender their weapons."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1058
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you know what position that man held?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1058
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You didn't know what position he had in the municipality or the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1058
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, tell me, then, why did he come to your particular house? Was he a friend or relative of yours?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1058
utterances.text: He had a sister.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In your house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1058
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So he said that it had been agreed for the Muslims to hand over the weapons they owned. Those people who broke into the cellar in Zvornik told us that weapons should be handed in and that the men should be searched, and that is how they took out the men.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Can I remind you, please, both the witness and Mr. Milosevic, remember that this has to be interpreted, so can you leave breaks between the questions and the answers. Now, you should have that in mind, Mr. Milosevic, because you've done it often enough before, but it will be new to the witness, but can you both leave breaks.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I was saying that he told you that the Muslims should hand over the weapons they possessed, because I'm reading from your statement in paragraph 7: "He told us that an agreement had been made for the Muslims to hand over their weapons." Is that right, Madam 1058?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1058
utterances.text: He knew that we didn't have any weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I not entering into that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1058
utterances.text: But I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But that's what you said in your statement, and you confirmed it a moment ago and signed it. So you don't remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1058
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. But he also advised you to leave Zvornik. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1058
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Though you yourself claimed that you had more friends among the Serbs than among the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1058
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, do you know what he had given similar advice to other Muslims?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1058
utterances.text: Those of us who were in the cellar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. So only to you who were there, that's how you know. That's what you know about.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1058
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 8 you say the attacks started in the afternoon of the 8th of April.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1058
utterances.text: In the evening, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We didn't hear that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Can you repeat the question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Are you quite sure that the attack on Zvornik, as you describe it in paragraph 8, commenced on the 8th of April? You are specifying now in the evening of the 8th of April.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1058
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And that is when you went to the cellar of your building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1058
utterances.text: No. We went before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Before that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1058
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What -- what prompted you to go into the basement before then if the attack started later? Had you been informed about the conflict beginning?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1058
utterances.text: Because they were saying that we should seek shelter in the basements, that we shouldn't go outside, that we shouldn't walk in the streets, that we should seek shelter in the basement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And who told you that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1058
utterances.text: Well, on the radio there were such announcements.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That was radio Zvornik, I assume, the local radio.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1058
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And that is when you went to the basement of your building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1058
utterances.text: It was a Sunday, I don't remember the date, when we went down to the basement, and we stayed there throughout.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As you say, there were another 12 or so men, 15 women and children; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1058
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you spent the night there up until 10.00 a.m. on the next morning, that is the 9th of April; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1058
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, the men who were with you that night, did they leave at all?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1058
utterances.text: No. No, they didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So they stayed in the shelter all the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1058
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And as Mr. Kahn noted a moment ago, none of them were armed; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1058
utterances.text: No one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you're quite sure of that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1058
utterances.text: Quite sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then about 10.00 you say there was a strong detonation which caused the door to break down and ten men broke in, wearing camouflage uniform, you say.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1058
utterances.text: Ten or so. I can't be quite sure about the number, but ten or so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Can you describe those camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1058
utterances.text: You know very well what camouflage uniforms looked like. You know that very well. Black. And you could just see their mouths and eyes. Those were the caps which covered their faces, with slits for eyes and mouth. You know that very well. I don't need to describe them to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What did they want from you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1058
utterances.text: They wanted the men to come outside, allegedly to be searched.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How many of them were speaking?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1058
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say that by their accent, by their dialect, you judged that they were from Serbia. So you must have heard them speak.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1058
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Two or three of them. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You can't say what the others were on the basis of their speech?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1058
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And is it possible that some of them were locals?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1058
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. You say that you were separated from the men, and the women and children were ordered to move towards the SUP of Zvornik, and the men stayed behind in front of the entrance to the building. Is that exactly how it happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1058
utterances.text: Yes, exactly so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, tell me, please, how much time went by until you heard the shots.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1058
utterances.text: Five minutes, not more.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How far had you gone in those five minutes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1058
utterances.text: Maybe 200 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: At the time, you didn't know what had happened to the men from your building; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1058
utterances.text: They opened fire when we had moved away, some 200 metres away, they started shooting. I started -- I wanted to turn around, however, the soldier was pointing his automatic rifle at my back.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you didn't manage to turn around, and you couldn't see anything.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1058
utterances.text: No, they didn't let me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 11, you say that moving towards the SUP you saw the body of Hakija Sehic and Fehim Kujundzic, but you're not sure of that because you couldn't see properly.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1058
utterances.text: I am sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now you're sure?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1058
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sure. I saw them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But as you say here that you didn't see it quite well, how is it that you're quite sure that it was one of these two?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1058
utterances.text: Of course I'm sure when they were my neighbours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then you say that you saw a certain Izet. From what distance did you see him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1058
utterances.text: About 400 metres. This is all one street.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. And how is it that you're sure from such a distance that those were all bodies of Muslims and there wasn't a single Serb?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1058
utterances.text: There was no distance; it wasn't far away.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. How far away it was is relative. You go on to say that you were sure that Arkan's took part in all these killings; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1058
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Where were the local Serbs throughout that period of time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1058
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you see anyone?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1058
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say that those same soldiers broke into a sweet shop and distributed sweets to children. Were there Muslim children among them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1058
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So they were killing Muslims and giving Muslim children chocolates and sweets.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1058
utterances.text: Yes, to learn from the children whether there were any weapons, who had those weapons, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Why were they giving them sweets?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1058
utterances.text: Because you know what children are like; they wanted to learn from the children things.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How do you know that they questioned them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1058
utterances.text: I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you heard them questioning the children?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1058
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And later on a Serb woman that is mentioned here by the name of Vera, so I won't read out her surname, and two Muslim women, Raza and Sadija - is that right - and a third, Zuhra, told you that they had seen dead people in front of your building; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1058
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And it was then that you had no doubts as to the fact that they had been killed? That they had been killed; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1058
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, tell me, please, a week later you went to Zvornik again with your sister from Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1058
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: To find out what had happened to all the people who had been with you in the cellar; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1058
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then you say that you spoke to a person called Dragan Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1058
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And that after looking through two lists, he told you that he hadn't seen the names of any family members that you were looking for on those lists; is that --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1058
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So what was the conclusion you drew from that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1058
utterances.text: What had happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Since you're speaking about wires and things, does that mean that the men who were with you in the shelter were first tied up?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1058
utterances.text: I didn't see it, so I can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you didn't see anyone tying them up.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1058
utterances.text: I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you heard shots five minutes after you had left the house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1058
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Madam 1058, tell me, please, when did you see this person whom we mentioned -- of course you can't remember these numbers. The pseudonym is 1237 of this person. When did you last see this man after he came to see you after the negotiations? I don't want to mention his name as he is protected.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1058
utterances.text: I never saw him again since then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: After he had told you to surrender your weapons and to leave?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1058
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As he's a protected -- do you know that he was a witness here sometime ago?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1058
utterances.text: No, I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: He testified here, saying, among other things, that he personally saw, from a distance of 500 metres, your husband and son being killed.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1058
utterances.text: Many people saw it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But that differs very much from what you are saying. Where are the other ten people, then? He was talking about seeing the two of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness can only say what she saw. Now, whether somebody else claims to have seen something different from 500 metres away is maybe a matter of comment, that's all, but the witness can't answer as to what somebody else saw.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, this is allegedly a witness of the killing, the testimony of an eyewitness, and quite clearly these facts differ.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Are you seriously suggesting that this witness is not telling the truth in describing what happened when her husband and two sons were killed? Are you suggesting that?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, I just wish to establish what truly happened, and the witness herself says that she didn't see it. All she knows is that her family members were killed, but she doesn't know under which circumstances nor where or how. She just assumes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. But -- just one moment. She saw them lined up, facing the apartment building, with their hands on their heads. She then heard the gunfire. Now, that is what she can say. Subsequently, they were killed or they were killed at the time. But she can't take it any further. That's her evidence. That's what she said happened. Now, if there's any doubt about what happened, then of course you can make a point to us. It will be up to us to decide. But I don't think this witness can take it very much further. She said what she saw, and there's no doubt that these men were killed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The only question is whether they were killed in battle or somebody shot them in cold blood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Are you seriously suggesting that these men were in some sort of battle? Is that what you're seriously suggesting, and that this witness is not telling the truth about her husband and two sons? If you are, you should say so, so that she may deal with it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, I cannot claim anything with respect to Zvornik because I don't know, but we do have two different statements by this witness and Witness 1237.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There is no point -- there is no point arguing about it now. It will be for us to decide if there's any significance in these differences which you claim. But really, we shouldn't detain this witness here any more, but if you're suggesting in any way that she is not telling the truth about what happened to her husband and two sons, then you should say so.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not have any information about this, Mr. May, as to what happened to her husband and her sons, but I do have information about what the witness has been saying and what this other witness said who is an alleged eyewitness. There is a major difference involved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That is what you say. It will be a matter for us to say whether there is any significance. Now, have you any other questions for this witness or not?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do have a few questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: A very direct question, Madam 1058: Are you sure that your husband and son were not participants in the battles in Zvornik and around Zvornik on that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1058
utterances.text: One hundred per cent certain. I vouch that with my very own life.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I never found out where they were. Had they had any weapons, they would have been in the woods, they would not have been in the cellar. You should understand that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Since they were not found, it could not have been established how they lost their lives. So you do not have any information about that, do you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1058
utterances.text: You ask Grujic where he moved them, from one graveyard to another grave and then to a third grave, where they were being taken from one grave to another. It was Grujic who did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I can't ask him about that. I don't know about him moving people this way.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1058
utterances.text: Well, I know that he did move from one grave to another.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Madam 1058, you left Zvornik on the 9th of April, 1992; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1058
utterances.text: Yes, when I was expelled.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And a week later, you came back and again the same day you went back to Bijeljina; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1058
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you only briefly returned on that day a week later.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1058
utterances.text: I could not have stayed when they were expelling all Muslims, expelling and killing them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you live in Zvornik nowadays?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1058
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And during the war, did you come to Zvornik again?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1058
utterances.text: I came when they asked us to come and to report in order to receive accommodation, but they killed many, many people, then caught them and killed them. I didn't mention this in my statement. It's not in the statement. I said it now so that you'd know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. When was this that you came to Zvornik again?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1058
utterances.text: In the beginning of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What year?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So a week after the 9th of April you were there and the beginning of May yet again?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1058
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Why did you come again in the beginning of May?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1058
utterances.text: They asked us to come and to register with the SUP, allegedly, in order to receive accommodation. People who had houses, apartments, were supposed to register their names so that it would be known that they were alive so that they could get their property back or give it up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So did you register there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1058
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Why didn't you stay in your own house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1058
utterances.text: I couldn't stay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Could you please explain this? I don't understand. They asked you to come to register there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1058
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And to continue living there normally?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1058
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So why didn't you stay?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1058
utterances.text: Well, they killed everybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Oh, they killed everybody who came back?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1058
utterances.text: Yes, all of those who registered and who stayed on. They were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How much time did you spend this other time when you were there in the beginning of May?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1058
utterances.text: Three or four days. It's not in my statement, and I don't see why you should ask me about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Although it's not in your statement, you are speaking about it now.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1058
utterances.text: All right. I should make it clear that I know everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I do want it to be established, what actually happened, that is. Now, tell me, please, you recognised some people here in some photographs. I received this file of yours.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1058
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The photographs of some persons whom you recognised.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1058
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And these are the people who barged into the cellar; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1058
utterances.text: Yes. No, not everybody. Arkan did not enter the cellar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not talking about Arkan. You could have seen Arkan on television.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1058
utterances.text: No, not on television. I saw him myself. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. So you saw him yourself. Tell me, please, how could you recognise these people who had been in the cellar if they, as you had described it yourself, had caps drawn down their faces with slits for the eyes and mouths only?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1058
utterances.text: Not everybody was masked. I already said that. There were some people who were not masked. They introduced themselves as being Seselj's men. Those who were not masked said that they were Seselj's men.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. That means that when you say that they entered the cellar with wooly caps with slits for the eyes and mouth, that pertains only to one part of them. The other part did not have caps.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1058
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So they were not masked.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1058
utterances.text: Yes, but they were together.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Why is it that you say this only now? In the statement you said that people with wooly caps drawn over their heads and faces with slits for their eyes and mouth, you mentioned that now.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1058
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you recognised them, they had these caps?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1058
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then you explained that some of them did not have caps.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1058
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How do you explain this now that some had caps and others didn't when in the statement you said that everybody was wearing a cap?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1058
utterances.text: I said that some did not wear caps. They introduced themselves as being Seselj's men, and they did not wear any caps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So when they barged into the cellar they said --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1058
utterances.text: Together. Together. Those who were masked, they took the men out and killed them. And those who were not masked dealt with us, the women and children.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. It may not matter very much how many of them were masked and how many were not. But just let me get this clear, please, Witness B-1058: Did these men say they were Seselj's men?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. 1058, I'm going to quote your very own statement to you. It's the end of paragraph 9: "As soon as the door opened, about ten soldiers barged into the room."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1058
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: "Wearing camouflage uniforms and wooly caps across their heads, and they pointed long rifles at us. The masks had slits for the eyes and the mouth, and some of them also wore black fingerless gloves, leather gloves."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you describe this quite clearly, that masked people came in.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1058
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now you say that some people who walked in were masked and others were not.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1058
utterances.text: Behind them were those who were not masked. First the masked ones got in and then the ones without masks. They were together. However, the first ones to appear at the door were those with the masks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That means those you recognised here in these photographs. I'm not talking about Arkan, he did not enter with him; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1058
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: They were behind them, and they were not wearing caps. They were not masked, and those are the ones you recognised.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: I apologise for butting in at this stage, but actually these questions regarding Seselj's men and who said they were Seselj's and who was participating in the cellar is covered actually in the addendum at tab number 3, where, if I may kindly direct you to the second column --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. If you'd go on. Yes. If you would just point out the passage so that we can all see it and hear it.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It's a passage which in the second column on the English at the tab, and it says: "When we get towards the SUP building, we were told to go into the library opposite the SUP building. The soldiers who remained in the library were abusive to us and cursed our mothers... They said that they were Seselj's men and that they were the good guys whereas Arkan's men had done the killings. We all knew that that was not true and that Seselj's men had fully participated in the killings themselves." So she's actually clearly stating that Seselj's and Arkan's men participated in the killings, and she's made this just to make it absolutely clear on this point because when she made her statement, she clearly omitted to say all of the people who were there. So she wanted to make this very point Mr. Milosevic is now making clear to the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mrs. 1058. These men you recognised are not among the ten or so who barged into the cellar with wooly caps on their faces?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1058
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Where did you see the ones you recognised? Could you explain that to me, because they're not ones with the wooly caps who barged into your cellar. Where did you see them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1058
utterances.text: I saw some in my sister's yard, sitting there. The next time I saw him in a house, the best man of my sister, his house.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When was this?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How did this happen when you just dropped in after a week to ask about these lists and you returned immediately?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1058
utterances.text: My sister's place in Bijeljina. He was sitting there in the yard.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1058
utterances.text: In Janja. He was sitting in Janja in my sister's best man's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Oh, I understand now. The people you recognised.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1058
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: One you saw in Bijeljina sitting in the yard of your sister's house and the other one you saw sitting in Janja.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1058
utterances.text: Yes. No, no, no, no. He was in Bijeljina -- I mean in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Where was he in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1058
utterances.text: I can't remember where I saw him in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You saw one in Janja. You saw one in Bijeljina. At the time when you saw this man in Janja and in Bijeljina, there were no clashes. There was no fighting. You saw some people just sitting there; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1058
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What did they have to do with the men who barged into your cellar with masks on their faces?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1058
utterances.text: Because he also had a higher position.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I don't understand what you're saying.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1058
utterances.text: He was holding a higher position.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Who was holding a higher position?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1058
utterances.text: The one I recognised.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Where did you see him, at which position? What is this office he held?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1058
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Again, Your Honour, I'd like just to make clear that this point about the recognition of photographs which Mr. Milosevic is making is again covered in the addendum in the final paragraph. And as you'll appreciate, the witness first made her statement in 1996. This is at tab 3. And at tab 3, it clearly states: "When I originally made my statement in 1996, I could remember what some of the people looked like who I saw enter the cellar, and I identified those I was shown pictures of which were attached to my statement." Which indeed they are. "However, due to the passage of time, I'm now only definitely able to identify Arkan in some of the photos which are attached to my statement." So she's clearly made it clear that more than -- nearly ten years has passed and her recollection isn't so good. She's trying to be honest about this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I shall be very brief, by think that it should be clarified for you, this particular matter that has to do with the recognition of these men and what they said there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The statement that you gave on the 28th and the 29th of September was, after all, quite soon after everything that happened, and here in paragraph 12 - so this is page 3 of the B/C/S version - you said: "Whether we got to the SUP building, we were ordered to go into the library opposite the SUP building. The soldiers who remained in the library were abusive to us and cursed our mothers and Alija Izetbegovic." And then you say here -- that's what you say in 1996. And later on you corrected it a bit: "They said that they were Arkan's men and that they were the good guys, whereas Seselj's men had done all the killings." So that's the way you had put it then, that they had said to you that they were Arkan's men. That is paragraph 12 of your statement. This is the first statement you gave, after all. Can you explain this to the Judges, how come this difference?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1058
utterances.text: I don't remember. Well, maybe I was so upset that I put it the other way round.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please, during those days about which you are testifying now, between all these sides, Muslims, Serbs, Croats, were there any conflicts at all?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1058
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Any -- did anybody get hurt or killed during these conflicts at all then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1058
utterances.text: In Zvornik during those first days, nobody had any weapons and there were no war operations. They were only all over the place killing people, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Was there a conflict round some hill? That's my last question.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1058
utterances.text: The hill Kula. There was some fighting there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So were there any victims there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1058
utterances.text: I don't know. This is a bit further away from where I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Madam 1058, when answering the questions from the accused, you spoke about the -- Mr. Grujic moving bodies from one graveyard to another and then to another, a third graveyard. Could you elaborate on that. From whom did you hear that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1058
utterances.text: People talked about this, people who were watching from Mali Zvornik. This is on the other side of the Drina only. They were watching through binoculars and the president was giving orders, this Grujic, this president, he was giving orders for this kind of transfer of corpses. People who watched this through binoculars from the other bank of the Drina River.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did somebody hear Grujic ordering such acts?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1058
utterances.text: He gave orders for everything. Everything that was going on in Zvornik took place on his orders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: No re-examination, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Witness B-1058, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the International Tribunal to give it. You are now free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, too, for having asked me to come and testify, to say the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Could you just wait while these blinds are lowered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just one moment, Mr. Groome. There's something I want to talk about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, there are two matters of evidence I could deal with. First, Mr. Van Baal, we will admit his transcript under Rule 92 bis, subject to cross-examination. There is one other matter which doesn't concern your part of the case but it would be convenient to deal with it since we were talking of it on our last hearing, and that concerns the statement of (redacted), (redacted), and there was a discussion as to whether the Trial Chamber may consider calling him. We have considered that and we shall not be calling him.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you would pass that on, please. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution calls Witness B-1610. He is the subject of protective measures, so I'd ask that he be brought in before we lift the blinds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The transcript should say the Trial Chamber would not be calling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you'd like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution will be seeking to tender one binder containing 12 tabs of exhibits. Could I ask that a number be assigned at this stage.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 532.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I ask we go into private session for a preliminary matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, your testimony has been received by the Chamber in written form. I only have one question for you in addition to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I would ask that the witness be shown Exhibit 532, tab 12. It is a photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And, sir, I ask you to take a look at this photograph and ask you: Do you recognise the person in that photograph?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: Yes, I do recognise him; it is Veljko Milankovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And Ms. Wee reminds me that I have forgotten something. Could I ask that the witness be shown tab 1 of the same exhibit, or a sheet. I'm sorry, we're a little bit disorganised this morning. Can I ask that the witness be shown a sheet, and I will ask that it be included as tab 13 of Exhibit 532.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, I'd ask you to take a look at that sheet of paper. Is that your name on the top of that piece of paper?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Milosevic, you can begin your cross-examination, but we'll break off fairly soon because it will be time for the adjournment, but you can certainly ask a few questions first.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. 1610, in paragraph 4 of your statement, which you gave on the 22nd of October, 2001, you say that you had never been a member of any political party; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you go on to say that even now you're not interested in politics; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: However, that's not true. You did become a member of the SDA party, and you said previously -- and I should like to draw your attention to that, Mr. May, that we took this formulation -- to the effect that you became a member of the SDA party during your stay in Germany.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: That's not true. That's not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You can check it out and verify whether this was what was stated previously. I can give you a detailed quote or, rather, the place you can find it, but I can't give it in open session due to the restrictions imposed. So what you said on a previous occasion about your membership in Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the SDA party in Germany in 1993 you actually knew when you made your statement in 2001. So why didn't you stipulate that then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: That's not true. I'm not a member of the SDA party.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So that means you stated that erroneously in a previous statement.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: I didn't say it. I'm not a member of the SDA party, or any other party, for that matter.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, you have all this written down and recorded, so I don't want to go back to that issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, you go on to say the following, and if you want me to tell you the lines and pages, I can do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Don't give the page numbers in open session. We can deal with that, if we need to, in private session. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 8, you say that in 1991, a certain man whom you say was from Knin, at a rally that was held of the SDS party in Prnjavor, addressed the Serbs that had gathered there and said that they should sell their last cow and buy weapons for themselves. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You, of course, did not attend that SDS rally, I assume.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, how come you can claim that that is what this man said, actually said?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: I claim that on the basis of what my neighbours told me who were passing by at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So there was an SDS rally, and some of your neighbours happened to be passing by and heard the man say that and then told you who the man was and what he said, and that is the basis you're testifying on; is that it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, you go on to say that in the Prnjavor municipality, the first checkpoints appeared in 1991. Isn't that right? You say that in paragraph 9 of your statement.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When was that in 1991 more exactly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: I don't know the exact date because I was in the Territorial Defence myself, so I can't give you an exact date. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, was it the beginning, the middle, or the end of the year? Can you tell us roughly? I know you can't tell us the exact date but you must have a rough idea of when it was during that year because you are testifying about it.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: Well, it might have been sometime towards the end of 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I see. The end of 1991. Right. And you also say in that same paragraph that most of those checkpoints were located next to a place inhabited by Muslims. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you mean to say that those checkpoints were erected in order to control the Muslims and not in order to provide security on the territory of the whole municipality? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: Because of the Muslims. And if you were Muslim, you had to have a permit to be able to pass through the checkpoint, a pass.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, as far as my information tells me, everybody had to have a pass to go through the checkpoints, not only the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: Yes, that is true, except for the fact that the Muslims were checked more strictly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I see. Now, these checkpoints, were they on the main road, the main road running from Prnjavor towards Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. They were also in Klasnice. There were checkpoints there too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. If they were on the main read from Prnjavor to Banja Luka, the main Prnjavor-Banja Luka road, that means that they were not erected and not located just beside Muslim villages. They were simply put up on the main road at all points where byroads connected with the main road. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: No. There was the village of Lisnja, that's where there was a checkpoint, towards Mravice. Right beside our village, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, all right. But all those roads -- and you have here in tab 2 a map of the Prnjavor municipality on which you can see that there are far more Serb villages than Prnjavor itself. You have the ethnic structure of Prnjavor there, and you can see that there were several times more Serb inhabitants there and Serb villages than there were Muslim villages and Muslim inhabitants and so on. Isn't that right, Mr. 1610?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then I'm sure you're -- you have in mind something that has been handed to me under the form of tab 3, and it says the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina as the header, Ministry of the Interior, Security Services Centre Banja Luka. That's what the document says. And it is sent to the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina, to the Assembly, to the government, to the Ministry of the Interior, and also to the Banja Luka Corps of the JNA, the Yugoslav People's Army. The date is the 23rd of September, 1991, and the document was signed by Stojan Zupljanin, chief of the security centre in Banja Luka. And the information is being sent reporting to the MUP corps, government Assembly, Presidency, and so on, and it states: "We are sending you information about -- on the activities of armed groups on the territory covered by the Banja Luka security services centre. Please find enclosed a report on that." And then it says that various forms of illegal activity are on the rise, are escalating, ever more numerous armed groups wearing uniforms and civilian clothing alike. And then it goes on to talk about ever increasing gunfire in public places, the mistreatment and abuse of citizens, the holdup and seizure of freight and passenger vehicles, shooting on active and reserve police officers, and it speaks about the general concern that this could escalate further, et cetera. So now, Mr. 1610, were these checkpoints erected in order to provide security, and does that follow on from this piece of information and document and what it contains, or are you saying that it was the Muslims who were controlled through these checkpoints?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: If there was abuse and mistreatment by the Serbs, then that -- then it was -- that Serbs could mistreat and abuse Serbs, that wasn't possible. They must have done it to the Croats and Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, judging by this chief of centre, Stojan Zupljanin, I would say that he was a Serb, especially as his first name is Stojan. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: All I can say is what happened in our parts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you whether he is a Serb. So is he complaining, as far up as the Presidency --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness may not know this gentleman. It would be doubtful if he does. But I think this would be a suitable moment to adjourn.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I address the Chamber briefly in private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Could I address the Chamber briefly in private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will go into private session. Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic, we're in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. 1610, in paragraph 9 of your statement, you say that most of the men at these checkpoints belonged to the Territorial Defence, that there were some military policemen as well; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You also say that you know that a captain, a captain from the Banja Luka region, was in charge of the whole region and that he issued the order to erect those checkpoints. Is that right? Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, tell me, please, were you too a member of the Territorial Defence at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And many other Muslims were also members of the Territorial Defence in those days, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: Yes. There were also five Serbs in my village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can see, you were a member of a TO unit which consisted of 48 Muslims and five Serbs; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: No. The total was 48.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Of which five were Serbs; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. The call to join the TO in 1991 was received from the military department in Prnjavor; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And your call-up paper, as you state in paragraph 10, was signed by a certain Meho Jasarevic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was he a Muslim too?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And like all reservists in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, you had a military uniform at home, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: I didn't have it at home, but we were given a uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what was the uniform like, Mr. 1610?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: Olive-grey green.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The customary military uniform, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Identical to those worn by JNA; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that at the time, from the TO warehouse, you were issued two machine-guns, some 50 M-48 rifles with 30 bullets each, and 150 bullets for the machine-guns?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: We were issued two machine-guns, M-48 rifles, and six or seven were not in working order.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But all this was happening in 1991, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now, tell me, in those days carrying out those duties in the TO, were you authorised to take into custody people who did not have licenses and were carrying weapons to search vehicles and patrol the village and its environs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: Yes. And there were two policemen with us who were also reservists.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And is it true that the TO unit, that is the one you were in as well, had been formed by that same captain whose name is Nedjo, as you state here, and who distributed the weapons to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: This came from the military department. The instructions were to maintain the law and order in our village so as to avoid any problems arising.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You yourself say there were 48 of you, of whom five were Serbs. How then can you claim that those checkpoints were erected to check Muslims when you yourself, as a Muslim and the other Muslims from your village, were also armed? In a large majority of cases you patrolled the village, searched people and vehicles as they went by.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: Not the surroundings of the village. Our duties were limited to the village and the side roads.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But the roads around the village. Your village is not the main road, is it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: Yes. Our village is -- lies close to the main road.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you were patrolling that area, searching and checking the population and passengers; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: Yes. You would notice a person driving something. We would check out whether he had any weapons. If he did, we would confiscate it and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So my question is: Why are you claiming that those checkpoints were erected to check Muslims?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: We had quite a lot of ammunition should there be any attacks, and the rifles were in order. So of course it was against Muslims. Others, for instance, in Potocani they had mortars, hand grenades.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But there were 48 of you, of whom only five were Serbs, and yet you say that the checkpoints were erected against the Muslims. So you -- there were 43 of you Muslims were organising checkpoints against Muslims, and you're claiming they were made there against the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: Well, of course they were against the Muslims, because first of all, the Muslims were in the minority there. And I am claiming that you had to have a special permit. You had to pay for it to be able to go outside of Prnjavor. So we couldn't move around anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not discussing the measures that apply to the population and the circumstances described by the chief of the security centre in his letter to the Presidency and other bodies. What I'm saying is that you in your unit had a majority, a large majority of Muslim members. Is that right or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: Yes, it is right that this was almost a purely Muslim village, the village of Lisnja.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you were armed, and you were part of the TO.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: Yes, we did have weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You certainly remember that in the area of Bosnia and Herzegovina in those days, the Yugoslav People's Army was still the only legal armed force, and Bosnia-Herzegovina was still part of the SFRY, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: Yes. I remember that very well. And the pull-out from Croatia and the five-cornered star that was replaced with the four S's.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not talking about the four letters. I'm just saying that the JNA was the only legal armed formation in those areas at that time. Is that right or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
