utterances.text: In paragraph 3 -- 13, you say that the first problem started in Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. March 1992 when you heard that at a distance of some 400 metres from your village automatic fire was being opened. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Before that there were no problems at all?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: Very minor ones. Nothing really dangerous.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then when you heard that, you were patrolling as a TO unit. You were armed, and you had all the powers that we referred to to stop people, to check them out, to maintain public law and order; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Why didn't you intervene or at least try to find out who had opened fire?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: How dared we go there? We had weapons, but we couldn't do anything with it. We would -- to get killed up there from Pavlovo Brdo from the Pavlo hill.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you didn't intervene?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: We didn't dare.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And did you inform anyone?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: Yes. We informed Captain Nedjo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was he in your village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So when he came to visit your village, you informed him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: Captain Nedjo would come on a daily basis to see us. He would come in the morning, shall we say, to inquire what had happened. We would report to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that you reported to him in writing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: This report was compiled by Nijaz. He was also a captain or something like that. He was an officer, and he would compile the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So this Nijaz drafted a written report; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: We kept record of events in a notebook as a patrol. Now, whether he was given this in writing, I couldn't tell you, but the two of them regularly met.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you have any of those written reports?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: No. I don't have anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. As I can see from your statement, you and the other Muslims from your village were armed with weapons of the Territorial Defence; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know of a single case that the Muslims without any cause opened fire? Did you report about that at all?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: Well, first of all, even if people tried to do that, we would prevent it from happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You claim in paragraph 12 in your statement that, "On one occasion when a drunken Muslim was shooting in the air, we had to take his weapon away," and you reported about that; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. We took his weapon away and we handed it over to Captain Nedjo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say that at that time you saw truckloads of reservists passing down the road through the village of Poraci, which belonged to Lisnja; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, you say that reservists who were transported in these trucks opened fire at the houses in your village. Is that your statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: Yes. The village of Poraci.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So they were shooting at random there.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: Yes, in passing. There is evidence of that which is quite visible. On the houses there are still scars, so to speak, but of course the windowpanes have been replaced.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, you say that there was frequent random shooting, as you had put it, but were any villagers killed or injured due to that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: Not at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So they were only shooting the way this man whose rifle you had taken away was shooting; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Were their weapons taken away too, the weapons they used to shoot around, as you had taken away the weapon of the person who had been shooting in the air?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: Who'd take their weapons away, the reservists weapons. We did report that to Captain Nedjo too. However, the same thing was repeated time and again, this very same thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But nobody got killed or injured.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. In the month of April, 1992, the captain asked you to return to machine-guns that you were issued with in 1991 as members of the TO; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And as far as I can see in your statement, that's when you stopped wearing a uniform, the uniform you had as a reservist; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But these rifles, they didn't ask you for them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: No. They didn't ask for the machine-gun ammunition either.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you kept the guns and the ammunition?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And now in paragraph 17, you say that in the beginning of May 1992, a written order came to the local commune, that is to say to your village. A written order, you say. This order indicated that all persons with hunting rifles had to surrender them; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, did this order arrive from the police or from the military authorities?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: It arrived from the police authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So it was a police order; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The army which was coming to the end of its tenure in Bosnia-Herzegovina had nothing to do with this order; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: I think that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now you say that soon after that, your village was surrounded by the police and by members of the unit called the Wolves from Vucjak; is that right? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When did this happen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: I cannot give you the dates. I already mentioned in my first statement that I cannot give any dates, but we were supposed to hand over these hunting weapons, and two or three -- we had two or three days to do that, and I had my brother-in-law's weapon and I handed it in.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. So the police unit was there and the unit belonging to the Wolves from Vucjak. So again there were no members of the JNA there; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: No, I didn't see any then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When did you first hear of this unit called the Wolves from Vucjak?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: Sometime in 1991. That's when I heard of them. But at that time I wasn't really very much interested in that, and I did not move about very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Had you ever heard of this certain Veljko Milankovic, the commander of that unit before that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: No, I did not know him personally. I did not hear of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you didn't hear of him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And who was in this unit the Wolves from Vucjak? Was that your local population from there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: It wasn't our local population there. There wasn't anyone from Lisnja or from the Muslim villages. I heard of this one man, Jansa, when all this happened in Lisnja. He was a Slovenian.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what about the rest? Where were they from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: I heard that they were from Ilova and places like that. Neighbours, from neighbouring villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Oh, from neighbouring villages.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you say that then when they surrounded you, you were told that you had to hand over all weapons; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: At that time, it was hunting weapons that had to be handed in.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So hunting guns had to be handed over by all weapons, whereas these members of the TO, including yourself, all still had normal TO weapons, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So when this request was made to hand over these weapons, was -- did it also refer to your weapons, the ones that you had as the TO when you were surrounded?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now let me not use this word "operation," but when this took place, when the village was surrounded, et cetera, was anybody killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. In paragraph 18, you say at that time about 100 sniper rifles were surrendered as well as a very large number of hunting rifles. Is that right? Is that the figure that you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: Yes. Because it was a big village and very rich. People were abroad for the most part and, of course, there were quite a few hunters there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So over 100 sniper rifles and a very large number of hunting rifles in your village, and all of that because they were hunters?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. In paragraph 19, you claim that you, together with about 25 men from your village, went to the Prnjavor police station to turn in weapons and that you saw three trucks full of soldiers from Knin there. That's what you said. They were called Knindzas; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: First of all, it's not Prijedor, it's Prnjavor. And secondly, it is true that I did go there and that I saw these men from Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You went to Prnjavor, not Prijedor. And you saw three trucks full of soldiers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were they moving about or were they sitting in these trucks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: They were by the police station. They were outside. Some were also on the truck and some were standing by the truck.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say that they were swearing at you, asking why you were surrendering weapons. Is that what they asked you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I find it incredible that they asked you that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: It's not that they asked this directly. They were just saying, "Why did you hand over your weapons?" They said that it was a pity that we handed them over, that they should kill us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Oh, so that's why they asked you. All right. As far as I understand this, they were reprimanding you for having handed over your weapons. So you invented this, Mr. 1610.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: This is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. In the same paragraph, number 19, you say quite literally: "They wore camouflage uniforms. I noticed that they had Red Berets. On their sleeves they had some kind of patch. As far as I can remember, the patch read something like SAO Krajina. I did not know what this meant." Is that what you stated?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you noticed, as far as you could remember, as you put it yourself, that there was something like "SAO Krajina" written on these patches.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: Yes, because we did not dare look at them directly. We were afraid. Of course they were saying all sorts of things to us, and I managed to catch a glimpse of these yellow letters that said "SAO Krajina."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Are you sure that that's what it said because you say here as if it said -- so you did see some things and you didn't see other things. What did you actually see?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: I saw that "SAO Krajina" was written there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You saw that it was written there. And how come you know that they were from Knin? Did somebody tell you that or is this your assumption? Is that what you assumed then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: I didn't assume it. As we were entering the police station bringing in our weapons, there were two young men there from Knin, and they were also swearing at us, cursing our Muslim mothers when we were entering this one room where weapons were supposed to be handed over. I [redacted].

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm just asking you how come you knew that they were from Knin. Did they say that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: When they were saying that -- I mean, these two men were sort of wounded a bit, injured. So that is how they were registered there. That's what I heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Where did they register them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: At the police station in Prnjavor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And that's where you heard that they were from Knin?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: Yes, as I was entering this place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And you received certificates for each and every weapon that you handed over; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Already in paragraph 21, you say that three or four days later, you received information from the SDA representative that any hidden weapons had to be handed over and that the military would come to collect them.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When you say "the military," what does that mean? You are talking about the army of Republika Srpska; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: For as long as we wore the five-pointed star, we always thought that it was the army, but the army was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: However, these two groups of Muslims, there were about 30 of them, they did not return any weapons; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: No, it wasn't that they didn't return any weapons. They came and they collected these weapons without any ammunition, without any clips, nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. As far as I can see here, at one point in time they disarmed the members of the army of Republika Srpska and they seized the weapons that had already been surrendered, and they went to the hill called Vinogradije from there; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: Well, Captain Nedjo also wore a five-pointed star, and it was only natural; we still thought it was the Yugoslav army. And it is true they went towards Vinogradije.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. So these two groups of Muslims, they disarmed their weapons and they went with their weapons to Vinogradije; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: It's not that they had any big weapons or something. They took these weapons that the people had handed over. They took that and went to Vinogradije.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How many of them were there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: Say about 30 in two groups. I didn't really count them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: They were all Muslims? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And now you say that the attack on the village of Lisnja started this same day around 1600 hours. However, previously, there was an announcement by megaphone stating that all inhabitants had to leave the village and gather at the sawmill, as you had put it; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And it was said then that those who did not go to the sawmill would be considered enemies and therefore would be attacked; is that right? Is that what was said specifically?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: Yes, that's what was said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was this a warning? These two groups of Muslims that had collected the weapons and went to the hill called Vinogradije, was this a warning to the civilian population to seek shelter in case there was a conflict?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You say that in the area by the sawmill there were also some JNA officers in olive-green/grey uniforms that you did not know, and this Slovenian Jansa, as you had put it, who still works in the MUP in Prnjavor nowadays. Is that what you stated?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: When I made this statement, he worked there then. I don't know about now, but at that time he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. It doesn't matter that he's a Slovenian. He is a citizen from that area, because you say that he worked as a policeman in Prnjavor.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: He did not work as a policeman before the war

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was he in this unit called Wolves from Vucjak?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So he was not a member of the army of Republika Srpska; is that right? Was that a paramilitary formation or what was this unit, the Wolves from Vucjak?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: It was sort of a paramilitary formation, but they worked in concert, in agreement with the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When did the attack on Lisnja take place, on which date?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: I've already said that I do not know exact dates. Perhaps you can ask me something else and I'll answer your questions, but I cannot give you exact dates. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You talk about the Wolves from Vucjak and so on and so forth. Is it correct that you did not see any JNA officers at all but only members of that particular formation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: Yes, I did see an officer. I saw one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You wore the same type of uniform?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: I didn't have a uniform at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, not then, but before that you did, you had the same type of uniform. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: It was the same colour, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let me just take a look at something you said in your statement. You say in paragraph 25 that there was a Slovene there by the name of Jansa and he was Milankovic's deputy. I recently heard that he was working in the MUP in Prnjavor. I heard Milankovic asking the JNA officers if they would bring a multiple rocket launcher to the hill called Pavlovo Brdo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, tell me, a moment ago you said you'd never heard of Milankovic, and now you keep referring to him as being the commander of the Wolves from Vucjak. So let me ask you this. When did you hear about the unit and what did you know about it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: Immediately before the attack on Lisnja took place, a cousin of mine said, "Milankovic is here." I didn't know him personally, of course, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. but I heard Jansa talking - I was 10 metres away - Jansa talking to the officers and asking them to bring in a multiple rocket launcher.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, let's look at this: You said that you made a previous statement, and I'm quoting. You -- "He addressed the officer. I don't know who he was." That's what you say quite clearly. "I do not know who he was. I do not know his name either. But at any rate, he was an officer." Is that the statement you made?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then you were asked on this previous occasion the following question, whether you thought that it was an officer belonging to the army of Republika Srpska, and your answer was yes. Isn't that right, Mr. 1610?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: I did give that answer, because at that time I considered that it was all the Serbian army, as it was indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So on that occasion, you said that this person was an officer of the army of Republika Srpska. Tell me now this: Are you changing about these officers, changing them around depending on the purpose you're giving your statement for? On the one hand, you speak about the JNA, the Yugoslav People's Army. On this occasion, when directly asked whether it was an officer of the army of Republika Srpska, you said yes. Before that, you say you don't know who he was, you don't know his name, but he was an officer. Then you were asked whether he was an officer of the army of Republika Srpska, and your answer was yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: Yes, that is what I said. I'm not saying I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but then you spoke of him as being a JNA officer as well.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: I did say that because when all this was happening to us in Lisnja on that particular day, it was the Serb army, as far as I was concerned, so that's what I said. But he was wearing a JNA uniform and he had the five-pointed star.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The same one that you had had up until then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And in paragraph 27, you mention a man -- a name Tito Potok. Tell me, who was that man; a Slovene, a Croat, a Serb? Who was he, this Tito Potok?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: Tito Potok was a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then you say that he asked you to start up the engines of a vehicle and other things. What's that got to do with these events? I'm not quite clear on what you're referring to, a hotwire.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: When we reached the mill, sawmill, he asked us to ignite the engine, and I didn't know how to do that using a hotwire. And then later on I said I'd go and find somebody who would be able to start up the engine that way. I wasn't able to find anyone, so I went to hide among the women and children.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. So you fled. You escaped and hid with the -- among the women and children. But what has this got to do with starting up an engine with these hot wires? What's that got to the do with the events we're discussing? I'm not clear on that. Why do you bring that up at all in the context of these events?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: Well, they were going to take the car, seize it, because the car belonged to a man called Adel Pekic [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you didn't say that in your statement. All you said was that you were asked to start up the engine using a hot wire, and straight away you fled and hid among the women and children.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: Well, not straight away, several minutes later.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Several minutes later. And in the meantime the Muslims who didn't want to hand over their weapons, did appear and surrendered their weapons? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me now, did anybody beat them, mistreat them, abuse them in any way once they did appear, once they appeared?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: Well, when they were coming down from the Lisnja road, down the Lisnja road, two men were abused. They were hit with rifle butts. And then about 30 of them were taken off in trucks to Prnjavor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, why didn't you say that in your statement, that they were mistreated and beaten, these people? Why didn't you say that? Because it would appear from this statement that nobody beat or mistreated anybody.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: Well, I said that they were beaten.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, according to you, once they had surrendered their weapons, this man Milankovic gave orders that the village be shelled. Is that what you're claiming?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, does that mean then that there was an armed unit that still remained in the village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: No. There was no unit remaining in the village. Only the people working in the fields and didn't know what was happening remained, because they were far away from their villages at that time. So they might have stayed on, and the people who were sick and elderly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Then you go on to say that the wolves from Vucjak stormed the village and set fire to 76 houses. Is that what you claim?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Then you go on to say that this man who asked you to start the engine of that car bragged and said that he had killed three men whom you yourself buried later on in the village of Konjuhovci. So what is the truth? What is correct here?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: What is correct is that he told us in the morning that he had indeed killed three men and that he said he would kill some more people too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And did you bury anybody yourself?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: I did dig graves, and then a young Serb guy told us to get lost, that it would be better if we got lost.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you didn't actually bury anybody yourself.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: I dug the grave and then I left.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you see a single man who had actually been killed there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So who was that man? Go on, tell me what person you saw.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: There was Bajis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you saw this one man who had been killed.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: I saw three corpses being brought in in the car.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What were these people's names?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: There was Avdija and Bajis Halilic [as interpreted], and this young person of 17, young man of 17.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know how they were killed, how they lost their lives? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: No, I don't know anything about that, but I do know that they were killed, and I do know that there was a cross drawn on their bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, were they killed during the fighting that took place there or were they executed by someone? Which is it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: Well, there wasn't any fighting going on there. Not a single bullet was fired. There was no fighting, no combat.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And where did these people actually come from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: They were from Porac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So this village that you're mentioning now, was there any fighting there, any clash of any kind or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: No, there wasn't a clash of any kind.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So there was no fighting, no conflict in your locality; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: As far as my village is concerned, nobody shot a single bullet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not talking about your village of Lisnja, I'm talking about the area itself, the whole area. Was there any fighting there? How did these men come to be killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: I don't know how they were killed. All I do know is that their bodies were found and that they had to be buried in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. So you don't know how they were in fact killed. Right. Now, after this attack, you were allegedly shut up in a footwear factory for 35 days, in a shoe factory. That's what you claim.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: Forty-five days in actual fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, 45 days. And where is that shoe factory?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: In Prnjavor

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And who held you prisoner there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: There was the reserve police force.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I see, the reserve police force from Prnjavor. Did they beat you, did they mistreat you in any way while you were being held there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: Well, yes. The weekends were best, Friday, Saturday and Sunday. That's when they would attack us, beat us when they would come back from their shifts, but they didn't beat me because I fled. There were 387 of us in total.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you say nobody beat you personally?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: Not me personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was anybody killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: Alija Dzinic was there. He was all beaten up. His head was beaten in.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So of those 300 of you -- how many did you say?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: Three hundred and eighty-seven I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Right, 387. Was anybody killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, in paragraph 44, you state something that is very interesting, and I'm quoting you. "During that night when we were all rallied up to go to the sawmill, I heard that the soldiers had taken away three women to Suad Zukancic's house and that they raped her. Is that what you said, that you heard about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: I said -- actually, the story that was going around was that they were raped. What it says in the statement is that that was not true, that she did this of her own will.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But I will read the following sentence. "I believe that -- my opinion is that the women were not raped. They were having sex with the soldiers for money, and it's only when people figured out what they were doing that they stated that they had been raped." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, do you know of any similar cases, others? That is to say, that they had sex for money and then later on said they had been raped.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Fine. Now, in paragraph 45, you go on to say that you did not know Veljko Milankovic before the war but that others told you who the man was.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: Yes. On the day the attack on Lisnja took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, this next bit does not relate to the fact that you had any knowledge of him having the reputation of a criminal and having been prosecuted and things like that. Did you know anything about that or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: No, I didn't know anything about that, but I did hear about it later on, that he was found guilty for some offences. Perhaps -- I heard about that perhaps a year later.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but you heard about it before you made this statement; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, why, then, didn't you mention that reputation of his?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: Well, I didn't know that it was necessary for me to do so, whether I should speak about that or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, you claim that you didn't know who he was, and yet before you made your statement you learnt that he was in fact a criminal, but you didn't consider it necessary to say that in your statement; is that it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: Yes, that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But in paragraph 47, you also claim and state that you knew that this same man, Milankovic, after the public security station in Prnjavor had been taken over, was arrested and taken to Banja Luka; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So who arrested him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: The specials from Sarajevo, special forces from Sarajevo arrested him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So the police actually arrested him, the regular police; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And the others that took part in this, what happened to them? Did the authorities react to the unlawful conduct of any of these men from the paramilitary formation except for him, for the boss himself? If they arrested their boss and chief, I assume that they should have arrested the others too. What happened to the others? What do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: Well, nothing was heard later on until he was released, and I didn't know about this paramilitary unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And where were you yourself after that? Where did you go to afterwards?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: I was in the village of Lisnja. This was before the events that happened came to pass.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And when you were released, how long were you there you said? Forty --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: Forty-five days.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. So you were there incarcerated for 45 days. Where were you later, afterwards?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: We were released later on to Lisnja and I had a work obligation to perform.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So all of you were released after that and went on with your lives normally in your village; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: Yes, later on, but not all of us. Some of us stayed behind. Others were transferred to Tunjica in Banja Luka. Because my uncle was there and he died a year later. And we had a work obligation to perform later on. That we were free, we were not free; they would come in in the evenings to mistreat us, abuse us.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, sometimes I slept at home. Sometimes I slept in my shed. It was difficult to know where to sleep or when they would turn up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, did they take anyone away from your village or kill anybody?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: Well, somebody from the neighbouring village came by, a man named Serbes, asking for money, cars. He would seize cars. And another formation would turn up and they confiscated our tractors and agricultural machinery.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So this man came and asked you for money, did he, and he stole vehicles? He was a criminal, then, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: Well, he was in the army. Now, who he actually was, I can't say, whether he was a criminal or not, but he was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you know him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: I didn't know him myself personally, but it's in the neighbouring village. So a neighbour of mine told me that that's that man. And I have some land there myself, but I didn't see him myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What was his name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: Serbes was what they called him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Serbes. What kind of a name is that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: Now, whether that was his nickname or not I don't know, but that's what they called him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So apart from this criminal who came, did anybody else come to mistreat the inhabitants of the village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: Well, yes, they did. For example, there was all sorts of units and formations coming by, and we'd always have to try and escape and flee. We had no electricity, nothing else, and as soon as it grew dark, you would try and seek shelter somewhere and hide.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. But throughout that time were any of the inhabitants of the village killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: Not at that time, but later on, yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When did -- was somebody killed later on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: Well, I left, but I think it was in 1993. That's what I heard. A man --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, but you have no personal knowledge of that after that period of time. You weren't there; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think there's only one question that needs some more clarification, and it has to do with the point in time when members of the Territorial Defence in those days, as the witness has explained, were given weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you said that what happened was that members of the Territorial Defence in your area, that is, 48 men of which only five were Serbs received weapons; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And when you were interviewed in October 2001, you said literally -- I don't know whether you have the statement in front of you, but do you remember saying at the time, and I quote: "Since I was a member of the Territorial Defence, I had a uniform at home." This was a clear statement by you; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: When we were issued weapons, we also were issued uniforms, I mean coats.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: That's why I'm asking you. You were quite emphatic here. You said that you had a uniform at home. And then you added that the TO received two machine-guns on that day, that a TO truck came, distributed weapons and machine-guns. Everyone who was issued a M-48 received 30 bullets. Nowhere did you mention what you said today, that you didn't have a uniform. Wasn't it the rule for all people who were in reserve to have uniforms at home? Should the need arise, they would have it at hand, as you actually stated in October 2001.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: I didn't have that uniform because I was in Derventa. I belonged to a company of recoilless cannon, and I returned my uniform. I was in Germany. Then later on when these people who needed to be selected, who were serious, who didn't drink and so on, they were chosen to be given uniforms and weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But that is your explanation now. Earlier on, your statement was quite clear. Does that mean that people with officer ranks were given uniforms on that day with officer's insignia or did they have those uniforms at home already?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: I can't tell you about the others. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Just one more point. You also said earlier on quite clearly that you kept the M-48 rifles and that you were never asked to surrender the TO rifles, M-48s.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: Yes, until that day when Lisnja was attacked.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But you said that you never returned those rifles.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: No, I didn't say that we never returned them. But when Veljko Milankovic was cursing God and saying why hadn't the weapons been Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. collected when he saw the weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: This is my last question. I am again drawing your attention to what you said quite clearly in your statement on page 4, third paragraph. "They never asked us to hand in M-48 rifles of the Territorial Defence." Is that right or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: What I meant was that they didn't ask us to hand in the weapons until that event.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But you said that you handed in 100 snipers but that these rifles were never handed in.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: I don't remember saying that, that the rifles were never returned.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like to draw your attention to the portion of your testimony with respect to you testifying that you heard Milankovic ask a JNA officer to move some weaponry, artillery, I believe, up to a hill called Pavlovo Brdo. Now, Mr. Milosevic has suggested that or has actually put to you that you have changed the identity of that officer to suit the different purpose or different purposes. I'm going to ask that you look at page 5 of your statement, and I have put a yellow note to the precise portion that I would like you to review. After you find the sentence in your statement which goes to this very matter, could I ask you to read it for the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: "I heard that radio MUP --" no. "I heard that he was working in the MUP." Correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I believe it's the next sentence.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1610
utterances.text: "I heard Milankovic asking a JNA officer if they would bring a multiple-rocket launcher to the Pavlovo Brdo. They agreed and they installed on that hill a recoilless gun. From where I stood, I could see a multiple-rocket launcher and the recoilless gun on the hill."

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No further questions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This question, the question that I put to the witness, didn't have to do with the actions but, rather, the identity of the individual. In the statement, the witness speaks of a JNA officer, whereas earlier on he said, and I quoted: "He addressed an officer. I don't know who he was. I don't know his name, but he was an officer." And then in answer to a direct question from whoever was asking the questions, in answer to a question whether he believes that he was an officer of Republika Srpska, he answered yes. You can find this in earlier statements. That was the point of my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think we better go into private session as the registrar points out.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Witness B-1610, that concludes your evidence for now, but could you please be available tomorrow, we must ask you because of this mistake which is nothing, of course, to do with you, but it is necessary that you stay, if you would, overnight, and if necessary, we will ask you to come back tomorrow morning. We will be able to fit you in sometime tomorrow morning if there are any additional questions. Mr. Milosevic, will you indicate tomorrow morning whether there are any additional questions for the witness. Perhaps you would have a look at that overnight. Yes. We will put down the blinds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will be taking the next witness. Before he comes in, there's something I'd like to raise in private session, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, again while we're waiting for the witness to come in, could I ask for an exhibit number to be assigned to the transcript of prior testimony and related exhibits in the binder in front of you at tabs 1 to 5.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit number 533.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you'd like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And perhaps the remaining blinds could be put up. Yes, Ms. Pack.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Witness, will you give the Court, please, your name.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: My name is Mustafa Ramic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Mr. Ramic, did you testify in previous proceedings before this Tribunal in September of 1999?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll read a summary of that earlier testimony. This witness became mayor of Brcko in the 1990 elections. He was heavily involved in the formation of the SDA in Brcko. The witness and his brother attended the first official meeting of the SDA in Sarajevo in 1990 and became party members. The witness explains in his earlier testimony that the SDA came in second in the 1990 elections with 23 seats. The SDP, or Communist Party, won the majority of seats in the municipal parliament. They were a mixed group, that is, there were Bosniaks, Serbs, and Croats amongst them. After the election, there was a coalition set up by the SDA, HDZ and SDS. The Executive Council comprised three SDA, three HDZ, and three SDS members. The witness describes the various posts in the municipal government occupied on a parity basis by Serbs, Muslims, and Croats. The highest ranking position was occupied by the witness; he was president. Lasting for several months before the war broke out, the army was distributing weapons among the Serb population in villages in Brcko municipality. For about a month or two before the war, there were 300 or even 400 men in the town of Brcko who were not from the area. The witness telephoned the JNA commander repeatedly about what was happening. He also went to see him to ask why tanks were digging in and groups with machine-guns deployed around the town. It was particularly odd that most of these weapons were aimed at the town. The JNA commander would not discuss it. He would say from time to time that these activities were being conducted also as a defence against incursion of some foreign forces from Croatia. The witness proposed a joint unit made up of Serbs, Croats, and Muslims, but this was refused. The SDS wanted to partition the town. This was debated at a televised parliamentary session on the 17th of April, 1992. The SDA's position was that this was unacceptable. All the parties took part in the debate, and the conclusion was to allow the SDS to take out a part of the town and a part of the municipality and call it the Serb municipality of Brcko. Before this, in early April, the SDS had already proclaimed the Serb municipality of Brcko. By the 1st of May, 1992, when the bridges in Brcko were destroyed, there was not a single bridge across which you could go to Croatia. Two bridges were blown up in Brcko, the railway bridge and the bridge for vehicles and pedestrians. The railway bridge was also blown up within three minutes of the pedestrian/vehicle bridge. The blowing up of the bridges caused panic in the town. The witness had ordered that the pedestrian/vehicle bridge be protected. A group of policemen had been set up as a checkpoint there. They told the witness later that the people who had blown up the bridge were very well prepared, that they numbered 20, and that they were from Serbia. They had taken over the checkpoint. They waited until morning to activate the explosives. About 150 people were on the bridge at the time. They were all Bosniaks. After the bridges were blown up, the witness goes on to say in his earlier testimony that he went to a meeting with the commander of the garrison in Brcko at the barracks. The commander said that he would bring the army in to take control of all the more important points in town. He said that he would agree not to bring the army in if the witness went on television and succeeded in calming the people down. The witness agreed to go on television. During the broadcast, people telephoned in and said that the army was already entering town. At one point, people phoned up from the local community of the 4th of July and said: "The army is at present shooting at us." The witness asked the deputy commander of the garrison, who was with him, what this meant, given that the army had agreed not to enter town. The programme was interrupted and the witness left the television studio. He thought that if he had stayed, they would probably have killed him. The witness went ultimately to Gornji Rahic, which was in free Brcko. He spent most of his time there during the war. When the shooting started and the attack was launched by the JNA and paramilitary units, he organised the defence of the rest of the town. They succeeded in controlling part of the town and the southern reaches. The witness identifies by name prominent Bosniaks from Brcko or prominent members of the SDA who were killed on the first day of the conflict. He gives evidence about SDA membership and party structures in Brcko and supporters and members of the SDA who were killed. He identifies, by reference to charts, the sections of town, Muslim majority areas, which were occupied on the 1st of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think that's a convenient moment. We will adjourn now. Mr. Ramic, we're just going to adjourn for 20 minutes. Could you remember during this adjournment and any others there may be not to speak to anybody about your evidence until it's over, and that does include the members of the Prosecution team. Yes. We'll adjourn now for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have a couple of supplemental questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Have you finished with the -- your summary?

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You have. You don't want to deal with the rest of it. Very well. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Mr. Ramic, the JNA garrison commander to whom I referred in the summary, what was his name?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: His name was Pavle Milinkovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Do you know his rank?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: He was a lieutenant colonel of the Yugoslav army.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Mr. Ramic, I read out in the summary a summary of your broadcast at the television station in Brcko. You were accompanied by whom during that broadcast?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: It was Captain Momcilo Petrovic, assistant commander for security matters.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ramic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's the only supplemental matters I wanted to deal with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Ramic, when the conflict broke out in the municipality of Brcko, you were mayor at the time; right?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: I was president of the municipality of Brcko.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I see. President of the municipality of Brcko. So at the time when the conflict broke out, you were the most important political figure in the municipality of Brcko?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: A short while ago, when the summary was being presented, it was explained that the majority vote in Brcko was won by the League of Communists; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then you, the SDA, the SDS, and the HDZ joined up to form a coalition in order to topple them; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And after that, you had a conflict amongst you?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: No, that's not the way it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As you say on page 2 of your statement, in May 1990, at a meeting of the Party of Democratic Action in Sarajevo when the statute was adopted, together with your brother Ibrahim, you became an official of the SDA. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Actually, after this meeting, we were in the group of initiators that established the SDA in Brcko.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you are one of the founders of the SDA in Brcko?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: At the same time you were a member of the Main Board of the party?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was. I mean, I became one later.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The Main Board for all of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes, but that's what I became later.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Later, at the congress, which was in the month of September, as far as I can remember, of 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The same year?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: The same year, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That's the first time when the Main Board was elected; right?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you were actually a member of this first Main Board of the Party of Democratic Action that was elected?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Ramic. Bearing in mind all these positions you held, I assume that everything that happened in Bosnia-Herzegovina, notably in Brcko, is something that you are quite familiar with.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Well, I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And your brother Ibrahim Ramic, at the beginning of the conflict when you were president of the municipality, he was president of your party in Brcko; is that right? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And that's when the HDZ was constituted in Brcko and its president was Mijo Anic.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that the head of public security in Brcko, I mean the police at the time of the outbreak of the conflict, was Stjepan Filipovic?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What was his ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And the commander of the police was Zlatko Jacarevic, a Muslim; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Well, he was one of the persons who were in top positions at the SUP at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. All right. So his deputy was Ivan Krndelj; right?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: I don't think he had a deputy, but Ivan Krndelj was, I think, one of the ten or so - how should I put this? - top people of the SUP, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And Suvalija Tanic, also a Muslim, he was head of the crime investigation service in Brcko; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes. He was the chief of all the inspectors, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In your statement, you say that two or three months before the outbreak of the conflict in Brcko, members -- the Serb members of the Territorial Defence erected barricades and checkpoints around town and on the main roads that led into town and out of town; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't put it that way. That was done by the army. It was the army that set up the checkpoints, the barricades, on all approaches to town and around town. That's what the army did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This is what you say. I'm quoting your statement now. This is the last paragraph on page 5. "In addition to that, perhaps two or three months before the bridges were blown up, the Serb members of the Territorial Defence would erect roadblocks or checkpoints around the town and on the main roads leading out of town and in the Serb areas of town." So I've just quoted your own statement. I just wanted you to confirm that for me.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Actually, I have to give a clarification. There wasn't a visible separate organisation called the Serb Territorial Defence. There was the Yugoslav army, and within it was this -- let's call it the Serb Territorial Defence if that's what you wish to call them, but there were also some other paramilitary formations. However, at any rate, everything was under the command and organisational responsibility and control of the Yugoslav army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: At that time, as I know too, throughout Yugoslavia there was no such thing as a Serb Territorial Defence, but you say Serb Territorial Defence, that they erected roadblocks. Why did you put it that way then in your statement? Why is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you, perhaps I did put it that way, but the meaning of it is what I explained just now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: If that's the meaning --

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps the witness might be given a copy of the statement if there's going to be continued questioning on that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Refer the witness to that paragraph, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Here it is, Mr. Ramic. It's the last paragraph on page 5 where it says: "In addition to this, maybe two or three months before the bridges were blown up, the Serb members of the TO would erect roadblocks or checkpoints around the town and on the main roads leading out of the town and in the Serb areas of town."

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Well, now that I read this, I see that I meant something completely different. When I say members of the Territorial Defence, until that point in time there was a single Territorial Defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina. So Serb members from this Territorial Defence did that together with the military, with the army. I didn't want to say the Serb Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You also say that the JNA, just before the war, armed the Serb population in the surrounding villages. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But as you say yourself on page 6, because you are testifying on the basis of your written statement, in paragraph 5 you suggested that a multi-ethnic unit should be formed by way of a compromise in order to patrol the town and the municipality of Brcko.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes. I can give an explanation in this respect with the indulgence of the Honourable Court. This is what it is all about: Since it was quite obvious that the Yugoslav army together with the mentioned different paramilitary organisations that were ethnic Serbs only had control over all the entrances into town and all other communication routes that could have affected possible war developments. When I asked Colonel Milinkovic -- Lieutenant Colonel Milinkovic to explain what he wanted to achieve through this and what he was doing, then he explained, but I mean several times he did not want to give any explanations, but once he said that they did this because there was a possible danger of an attack. And I asked what kind of attack, and he said an attack from Croatia by the Ustashas. I'm paraphrasing now. Since of course this was not correct, and since in a way he just wanted to disguise his own activities, I suggested to him let's do the following thing, let us defend the town with a multi-ethnic unit consisting of Bosniaks, Serbs and Croats. Let us establish this kind of unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Ramic, wasn't the JNA such an armed force that consisted of all ethnic groups, at least at that time?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Formally it was before, and I used to be a member of that kind of JNA. But on the very eve of the war, it had turned into a purely ethnic Serb military organisation. That's the way we can put it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, as a consequence of all of that, you say that members of the Bosniak and Croat people started leaving town. I would like to draw your attention to page 7, paragraph 3. You say: "Members of the Bosniak and Croat communities started leaving town because they were so worried that war would come. I should add that large numbers of Serbs had left certain areas of town in mid-April. This was seen as further evidence that the Serbs were preparing for war." Now, please, Mr. Ramic, I quoted the entire third paragraph to you. You say that the inhabitants there, the Bosniaks and the Croats, were leaving town. And that this is because they were so worried that a war would break out. And you say that the Serb inhabitants were doing the same thing, but you understand that as further evidence that the Serbs were preparing for war. Now, please explain this to me. When the Bosniaks and Croats are leaving, that doesn't mean that they are preparing for war. And when Serbs are leaving, that is further evidence that they are preparing for war. How is it that you interpret the same thing in different ways in the case of different ethnic groups?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: What you quoted just now is perhaps not a very fortunate wording. Actually, it was this way: For a while, it was noticed that Serbs, ethnic Serbs, were leaving town. It would happen that overnight or, rather, the next day we would realise that certain people were no longer there, that they had left. This went on for a while, perhaps for about a month. And it was noticeable. It's not on my part or on part of the other officials in the municipality at the time, but all citizens noticed this and people started talking about this, why was it that members of the Serb ethnic group, the citizens of Brcko, were leaving town. Bearing in mind what was going on in time in the broader region and even closer to Brcko, meaning Bijeljina, Zvornik, Bosanski Samac, and many other things, bearing in mind again that, before that, the area of Croatia was already engulfed by war, so citizens who were ethnic Serbs obviously had an inkling that something bad would happen. People talked about it in town. It wasn't a political instruction or a pamphlet or I don't know what. Quite simply, the people came to that conclusion on their own. So it was at their own initiative that Bosniaks and Croats slowly started withdrawing their own family members from town. That is what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Well, that's the point precisely. You say that both Muslims and Croats and Serbs leave town. However, when the Muslims and Croats leave, you say that this is because they were worried. And when the Serbs leave, you say that they were preparing for war. Does that seem logical to you, Mr. Ramic?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: I think it is very logical. Please, Mr. Milosevic, there is the following explanation: From some parts of town, citizens of Serb ethnicity started leaving slowly for reasons unknown to us, and this had been going on for a while. At the same time, there was a war, and also there were war crimes that were being committed, and this news had reached Brcko, and everybody knew who was doing all of this. The reaction of the citizens belonging to other ethnic groups was that the same scenario was being prepared for Brcko too, so let us take care of our family members, and let us get out of here and move to a safer area. That was the gist of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: If that's the gist of it, then let's go on. Finally war started in the area of Brcko when, as you had put it, the bridges were blown. That's what you say here.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. That was the beginning of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Very well. Tell me first of all, you certainly know where the Mujkici local commune is in Brcko.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And is it correct that in the territory of this local commune at the gas station on the Brcko-Loncari road, before the conflict broke out, there was a privately-owned company there, Mibo, and the Brcko brick laying factory.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Mibo was not a privately-owned company though. It was a state-owned company, if we can put it that way, until then, and also the brick factory.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: There was DDPSC there; right?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So was that company. And is it correct that in 1991, very close to the station where the -- where vehicles were overhauled, there was a shooting range that was built there?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: I don't know about that. Oh, just a minute. Perhaps you mean the shooting range of the association of marksmanship in Brcko. So this is a sports organisation that existed in Brcko. This was a shooting range, but real ammunition was not used there but the type that is used for sports events.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And is it correct that for months before the conflict broke out in Brcko it was precisely Muslims from this local commune of Mujkici, like from other parts of Brcko too, came to this shooting range in order to train in terms of shooting from automatic weapons and other weapons?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Oh, please. This has nothing to do with the truth. How could people have automatic weapons? Everybody would have noticed something like that in town, the police first and foremost. So in that case, the police would certainly react. I as mayor would have been informed about this certainly. I don't think this is correct at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. So you say you don't think that's correct. Now, do you know who Veljko Mensur from Brcko is?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do know him. He's a well-known sportsman. He was a boxer and karate player.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And was he one of the instructors, the training instructors there?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: No, that's not right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now I'm going to ask you to take a look at an Official Note by the public security station in Brcko, and it relates to knowledge about the activities of the SDA and HDZ in the local commune of Mujkici. And I'm just going to read out a short passage from that Official Note. It says: The DDPSC, which as you said a moment ago was set up in the Mujkici local commune behind the Brcko Loncari petrol pump and links Sefir Momimbo [phoen] and the Brcko bricklaying factory and is about 200 metres from the River Sava, within the frameworks of that company there is a new facility for vehicle repair with a large warehouse, and it is dug into the ground. We learnt from the employees that this warehouse or storage space was used by the Green Berets as a dormitory and a kitchen because we found large quantities of blankets and mattresses and beds as well as a fully-equipped kitchen. In addition to the warehouse, next to it there is a shooting range for which we have received information that particularly in recent months before the war conflicts broke out, was used for the training and shooting using infantry weapons. It was noted that large groups of Muslims from town and the Mujkici local commune would go there after 3.00 p.m. for shooting practice. And when asked what they were doing there by anybody, they would say that they were allegedly hunters doing some target practice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What is the date -- what is the date of the document that you're reading from?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The date of this document here is the 7th of November, 1995. It is an Official Note by the security station in Brcko. And it has a stamp as well up at the top. The Municipal Secretariat, it says. I assume for the interior.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Brcko municipality. You can have it, have the witness take a look at it. And I referred to the second passage that is marked in marker ink here. So you can take a look at that, and I'd like to have this exhibited.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness see it first.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the first time that I see a document of this kind and hear about it. That's the first thing I want to say. Secondly, this document bears the stamp of the 7th of November, 1995, which means when the war was already over, so this is a retroactive, fabricated, quite obviously, document. Proof of this cannot be so, is the simple explanation. That that part of town, the part of town you're referring to, was of a multi-ethnic composition; there were Croats and Bosniaks and Serbs living there. Had anything like that actually taken place, quite certainly the organised parts of the authority, the police force or other inspector services or similar services and ultimately the army must have known about it, because the army did have its own patrols that patrolled the area, and they would have had to have come across something like that. So this is something that I see here for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But it is an Official Note and it testifies about the activities prior to the beginning of the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: But, Mr. Milosevic --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It was drawn up later on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Milosevic, after the war you can write whatever kind of official notes you want as to what happened and how it happened. I'm now going back to the time just prior to the war, the breaking out of the war, that is to say before the 1st of May, 1992. And I deny that there is any truth in what this document says. Had any of that been true, then not only I myself as the mayor of the town would have known about it but army would have known about it too and so would the police. And neither of these two institutions told me about anything of that kind prior to the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll give it a number.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I have here, Mr. Ramic, another Official Note, another document which was written somewhat earlier on, in October. That's when it was compiled. And it says: "In Mujkici before the war broke out on the 1st of May, 1992, a new war hospital was erected equipped with equipment and medicines from the city hospital. Ibrahim Ramic headed these activities, the president of the SDA party." That is to say, your brother. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then Trumic Zijad, director of the county hospital; and Dr. Smail, an internist; the president of the SO of Brcko, Dr. Pitic Fadil, who was a surgeon; and others.
